Honestly, Prof Yu is a really solid choice. She’s definitely not the type to just stand there and read off the slides. She tries her best to keep things as simple as possible. The lectures is bit of a mixed, sometimes it gets a little boring, but sometimes she keeps everyone engaged by giving real-world examples or asking questions throughout the class.

When we were learning oligopoly, she used iPRS questions for practice and refused to move on until like 80% of the class got the correct Nash equilibrium. Math-wise, she even threw in some calculus (like the second derivative test) to show us how the models actually work. It’s not technically required for the course, but it honestly made the concepts way clearer.

Btw, she gave our session (L4-L6) an extra 30 minutes compared to the other classes during the final exam.

sections.content:
This course covers the fundamentals of economics (basic models like supply–demand, market equilibrium, elasticity, consumer/producer surplus, opportunity cost, and basic policy effects). The material is not conceptually hard, but it becomes “easy” only if you stay consistent. Topics build on each other, so if you fall behind for 1–2 weeks, later chapters feel confusing. Overall, the content is straightforward and very manageable if you spend steady time reviewing and practicing.
Planning tip: After each lecture, spend 30–45 minutes rewriting key graphs/definitions and solving a few short questions. That alone keeps you ahead.
sections.teaching: The teaching is clear and easy to follow. The instructor explains concepts step by step and uses simple examples to make ideas intuitive. Complex theories are broken into smaller, manageable pieces, so it feels less stressful and more engaging. The pace is steady, and it’s easy to understand what the instructor expects you to know for exams. Overall, the teaching style makes the material accessible and helps students build confidence.
sections.grading: Grading is mainly exam-based (midterms + final) with assignments contributing as well. Midterms are usually multiple-choice heavy (around 50–60 MCQs), and performance depends a lot on how many practice questions you do. The weighting between exams can help if one midterm goes worse, and the overall grading feels normal/standard for UST. If you stay consistent, getting a solid grade is realistic.
sections.workload: The workload is very light. Most of the effort is exam preparation and keeping up with lecture concepts. If you review weekly, you won’t need stressful cramming. Assignments are not heavy and are usually aligned with what’s taught.

sections.content: The course is mainly based on Principles of Microeconomics (10th edition) by N. Gregory Mankiw, published by South-Western, Cengage Learning. The material itself is very basic microeconomics. The lectures do not strictly follow the order of the textbook, and by the end of the semester we roughly reached the chapter on monopoly. As an introductory course, the content is actually quite thought-provoking and sometimes interesting, especially if you have never formally studied economics before. That said, as a core business school requirement, you do not really have a choice about whether to take it or not.
sections.teaching:
Li Xuan’s lecturing is honestly not very effective. She tends to look down while speaking, and although her pronunciation is fine, her pauses and sentence breaks can be quite confusing during lectures. However, her understanding of the subject is strong. When you ask questions after class, she explains concepts very clearly and in a fairly intuitive way. The issue is more about in-class delivery than ability.
In contrast, Victor’s tutorials are very well structured. He does a great job highlighting the key points, walking through examples step by step, and making the logic behind each concept very clear. Concept comparisons and distinctions are explained thoroughly. After the first midterm, I stopped going to lectures and only attended tutorials. My personal approach was to go through the lecture material on my own and then rely on tutorials, which turned out to be quite efficient for me.
sections.grading:
The grading is very student-friendly, and there are two different schemes you can choose from.

Scheme (1): Two midterms
Problem Sets: 10%
1st Midterm: 15%
2nd Midterm: 15%
Final Exam: 60%

Scheme (2): One midterm counted
Problem Sets: 10%
Higher Midterm: 25%
Final Exam: 65%

Personally, I scored 54/60 on both midterms, 84/100 on the final, and got full marks on all problem sets, which resulted in an A+. Overall, the grading is quite generous, and the instructor clearly tries to help students perform well.
sections.workload:
The workload is relatively light. There are ten problem sets in total. If you complete them on your own, each usually takes around 1.5 to 2.5 hours, depending on your background. Of course, if you simply look up answers online, half an hour is probably enough. Personally, I do not think the problem sets are very helpful for the final exam.
Both midterms are multiple-choice. Before the exams, I did as many past paper questions as I could find, probably over two hundred in total, which helped a lot with exam familiarity. The final includes both multiple-choice and written questions, and there are no past papers available. My approach was to use AI to generate concept comparison questions, since Li Xuan’s exam style is quite textbook-based and focuses heavily on definitions, concepts, and some logical extensions. The written questions are relatively challenging. My suggestion is to fully understand the provided sample questions. Even though the actual exam questions are not very similar, working through the samples helps you get used to the question types.

sections.workload:
There is 11 problem sets, and the best 10 will be used to calculate your grades.
Problem sets are graded ON EFFORT but NOT CORRECTNESS. As long as you answer all questions, you can get full marks.
They don't even care whether you use AI or not, they explicitly say AI is allowed in HW in course outline pdf.
You can form a group of 4 to complete each problem sets together. That means you only have to do 1-2 questions in each problem sets, which is not a very heavy workload.

Also, as mentioned, because both mid-terms and finals are open-book, so what you have to do is just understanding concepts, but not memorizing.

Tips for students aiming at high grades:
1. Do all questions in problem sets. Even I am doing problem sets in a group, but I still try all questions on my own in my spare time. Doing questions help you get better understanding on concepts.
2. Remember some important concepts even it is open-book. It saves your time on finding concepts in your note during final.
3. Don't simply print all powerpoint slides. Try to summarize the content in the slides as your own note documents and print your own note during final. It helps you to have better understandings on concepts and reduce the number of pages of your notes.

I also upload my note that I use in my midterm1, midterm2 and final. I don't promise they cover all points that you need, and I don't promise they can help you a lot.
But if you really don't have time to write your own note, and you don't want to read so many slides, then you may use them for your reference.

sections.content:
Microeconomics is the branch of economics that focuses on individual agents, such as households and firms, and their interactions in markets. Here’s an overview of the key concepts and topics typically covered in microeconomics:

1. Basic Principles of Microeconomics
Scarcity and Choice: Understanding the fundamental economic problem of limited resources and the necessity of making choices.
Opportunity Cost: The cost of forgoing the next best alternative when making decisions.
2. Supply and Demand
Law of Demand: As prices decrease, quantity demanded increases, and vice versa.
Law of Supply: As prices increase, quantity supplied increases, and vice versa.
Market Equilibrium: The point where supply and demand curves intersect, determining the market price and quantity.
3. Elasticity
Price Elasticity of Demand: Measures how much quantity demanded changes in response to price changes.
Price Elasticity of Supply: Measures how much quantity supplied changes in response to price changes.
Income and Cross Elasticities: Understanding how demand changes with consumer income and prices of related goods.
4. Consumer Behavior
Utility Maximization: The concept of consumers seeking to maximize their satisfaction from goods and services.
Budget Constraints: How consumers allocate their income to various goods and services.
Indifference Curves: Graphical representation of consumer preferences and trade-offs.
5. Production and Costs
Production Functions: The relationship between inputs (labor, capital) and output.
Short-Run vs. Long-Run Costs: Understanding different cost structures and their implications for firms.
Economies of Scale: The cost advantages that firms experience as they increase production.

I had taken Economics before university, and thus the content was a piece of cake to me, but to other students, I would say that this course is easier than most courses in HKUST.

The contents are actually very intuitive, but still useful in daily-life. Things like demand & supply, Nash equilibrium and Game Theory, and different markets and its equilibriums is what I think is basic knowledge, and its very good to know if you have not done your own studies on them.

The course outline states:
As an introductory course, this course will cover the fundamental concepts and tools involved in microeconomic analysis. Economics provides a powerful way of thinking that helps you
to understand many human and social phenomena. Real-world examples and cases will be used as much as possible to enhance your understanding.

"Principle of Microeconomics, Ninth edition” written by N. Gregory Mankiw, published by South-Western, Cengage Learning.

The pace of teaching is indeed faster than previous semesters (from an experienced TA) as Prof Siu seldom shares life lessons now. You can expect to finish one chapter per 1.5 weeks and in total ~10 chapters

sections.teaching:
From my point of view, Prof Siu is a decent professor. He is very willing to answer students' questions, and (in my opinion) explains concepts in a fun & clear way. You can bombard him & TAs with emails and receive detailed explanations the next day.

But indeed, his style is not for everyone. He likes sharp and swift responses and sometimes will push students further to perfect their answers, which may come across as intimidating

He also has an emphasis on 'system of thinking' and does not really like drilling papers. Hence, his questions are mostly scenario-based and you need solid understanding instead of memorization/drilling, which is fun if you love intellectual stimulation but not that exciting if you only strive for the grade

The final score of the course is the higher of the two scores obtained from the following calculation methods:

Method 1:
Assignment: 15% (ignore the lowest 2 scores)
Midterm 1: 12.5%
Midterm 2: 12.5%
Final exam: 60%

Method 2:
Assignment 15% (same as above)
The higher midterm: 22.5%
Final exam: 62.5%

Basically, if you do particularly well in one of the midterm or final, method 2 will be in favor of you.

Due to online mode of teaching and exams, the two midterms consist of 50 MCs each. This makes the mean rather high (about 80%), so revisions and hard work is really needed. Exam is designed to be long and demanding (which is the original wordings of Prof. Li who says this could increase the opportunity cost of cheating, which I think is reasonable). Turns out the mean is quite low (about 50%). As everyone has a not-so-high score, you don't need a very high marks to get a prominent grade.

At last, attendance is not counted towards the grade, but it is not advised to skip the lessons. They are really useful.

For me, I have done all assignments and +1sd in one of the midterm and the final, and turns out an A grade, which is good enough for me as a newcomer in the world of Economics.

Extremely Competitive

Don't underestimate the course just because the content is easy, cuz everyone will get relatively high marks (mean for midterms and final: 85+). So if you are below mean in any exam, well your grading will be devastating.

Since the score difference between every student is so low, even a tiny difference in marks will result in maybe 1-2 sub grade differences.

sections.content:
Course Description: As an introductory course (it may be your first course in economics), this course intends to coverf undamental concepts and tools that are used in microeconomic analysis. In this course, I will show you that economics provides a powerful way of thinking that can help you understand many human and social phenomena, and also enrich you in a wide range of career choices. I willuse real world examples and cases as much as possible in order to enhance your understanding of course materials.  Eventually, I would like all of you to come up with your own “definition” or“meaning” of economics and establish its applicability in your daily life.Textbook:“Principle of Microeconomics, Seventh edition” written by N. Gregory Mankiw, published bySouth-Western, Cengage  Learning.    Supplementary  readings  will  be posted on the CourseWebsite (if any).Learning Outcome – School Intended Learning Outcomes (“SILOs”):1.Explain the methodology of microeconomic analysis, including key assumptions used,how economics differs from the other social science disciplines, and the strengths andlimitations of this analysis framework (SILOs # 1 and 4). 2.Describe the key concepts and tools of microeconomic analysis, such as gain from tradeand   specialization,   how   price   is   determined   in   the   free   market,   how   efficiency   ismeasured, how the market structure affects the determination of price and quantitytransacted, and decision-making by buyers and producers under constraints (SILOs # 1, 3and 4).3.Examine the role of government and its interaction with the free market by evaluatinggovernment   policies   and   their   impact   on   economic   activities   and   justifications   forgovernment intervention or participation, such as to maintain the public good (SILOs # 1,3 and 4).1
4.Apply economic tools and principles to identify, analyze and propose explanations forand solutions to real world issues (SILOs # 1 3 and 4). For the details of SILOs, please refer to: http://www.bm.ust.hk/sbmlearn/eng/thirdcat.php?sid=5&thirdid=3Course Format / Teaching Approach:This course is delivered through lectures and tutorials. Students attend two 80-minute lectures perweek.  Personal Response System (PRS) will be used during lectures to encourage class participationand sharing among students and with me. Please try to attend all lectures and participate actively indiscussions. Tutorials will be arranged when needed. Teaching       &       LearningActivitiesRoles in the CourseSILO AddressedLecturesExplain   key   concepts   and   theirapplications; Cases and examples tobuild student’s critical and analyticalability1,2,3,4In-class Q&A through PRSEncourage class participation, criticalthinking and discussion1,2,3,4TutorialsReview   and   further   illustration   onimportant   topics,   practice   problem-solving,   encourage   discussion   andparticipation1,2,3,4Quizzes & Problem SetsEnhance   understanding   of   coursematerials   and   their   applicationthrough practice1,2,3,4Use of Personal Response System (PRS):PRS will be used in lectures.  In order to get a PRS handset, please visit the following website forinformation: http://celt.ust.hk/teaching-resources/teaching-clickers/faq-students.  The use of PRS isto   encourage   classroom   participation,   discussion   and   sharing   among  students and with   me.Questions will be asked in lectures and the PRS allows you to respond in real time.  A summary ofanswers will be shown and shared. Examinations and Grades:Quizzes and Problem sets:You will be assigned 10 quizzes and 3 problem sets during the semester.  Quizzes (MCQsonly) are assigned on a weekly basis and submitted on the canvas. Each quiz remains activeon the canvas for one week. By default, only one attempt is allowed. The make-up arrangement canbe in  the form of written-exam, oral exam or research paper, etc. Please NOTE that theinstructor has the final discretion on all arrangements of the make-up exam.  Students whorequest for the make-up final exam should comply all the requirements as communicatedby the instructor.  Failing to meet any requirement may result in a ZERO score.3

sections.content:
The content starts off very easy but gets much harder as it progresses. Those marked with  are easy topics. But starting from topics marked with , such as the cost curves in firm production and firms' decision under different market structures, rigorous mathematical and graphical reasoning are required. In these topics, you will see different curves intersecting seemingly randomly like a fountain (but indeed with a rationale behind), and what math noobs can do is to stare at the lecture ppts and remain puzzled. So this course isn't really for math noobs.

Topics included:
 Ten Principles of Economics
 Thinking Like an Economist
 Interdependence and the Gains from Trade
 The Market Forces of Supply and Demand
 Elasticity and Its Applications
 Efficiency of Market
 Government meets Market
 The Costs of Production
 Firms in Perfect Competitive Market
 Monopoly
 Strategic Interaction and Oligology

The final exam was an absolute mind blower compared to the strikingly easy midterms. It required us to answer long questions with full economic analysis backed by graphs and economic concepts. Algebraic equations are needed in the oligopoly part and those who are bad at algebra can screw up the final exam easily.

DON'T TAKE THIS COURSE if you're a math noob!!!
sections.teaching:
Prof Siu Kam Wing might be popular among all the students as he often digresses, and turns his lectures into life lessons. Lectures were dominated by mainland students in the front rows and as they had much better mathematical reasoning than most of the locals, he resorted to a more mathematical approach in explaining the concepts, and what maths dumbs like me could do was just to freak out and stay confused.

The TA is from ECOF and his tutorials are even more "mathematical" than Wing's lecture. He does the mathematical proofs of basically everything which isn't needed in the exams and the whole course at all. He fails to explain the very basic concepts and I doubt whether he himself actually understands them.

DON'T TAKE THIS COURSE if you're a math noob!!!

Marking is strict by the TAs and it is hard to argue with them in short questions and long questions.

*Terrible choice* as a common core or business minor requirement. Return on investment? Not good. There are better courses out there for you believe me.

sections.content: This course covers less detailed information compared to the 3-year DSE Economics syllabus but includes new topics like the cost and production curves. The scope is designed for those who have not studied Economics in secondary school, and the concepts are explained using simple daily life scenarios to make them easier to understand even for beginners. However, after the midterm, more complex topics are introduced, such as elasticity of demand & supply, cost and production curves, monopoly, and game theory.
sections.teaching: Prof. Siu (usually referred to as Wing) is a very humorous person who often makes jokes and talks about his interesting experiences in life. He can also explain the concepts in a way that makes us easier to understand, by using metaphors and daily life examples. Despite his funny Chinglish accent that requires more concentration to understand, his explanations are clear and precise.
sections.grading: This course is quite competitive if you are taking it as a common core, since it is a business core for sbm students and partially affects their major selection, so they will work extra hard to push up their grade. Even as a common core, if you are planning to put minimal effort on it like you may treat other common core courses, then you may end up with a bad grade so be warned. It is not difficult to get a B range as long as you understand the concepts taught and have handed in all the homework problem sets. But if you want to get an A range, then you will have to work very hard.
sections.workload: The workload is not very high, with just a problem set every two weeks from the textbook. However, the topics covered may be quite overwhelming throughout the whole course, as the final is cumulative. It is advised to focus on the topics after the midterm, especially the cost and production curves, as they are the main focus of the final.

For everyone who's not a born-genius, an actual workaholic, or being controlled by grades in order to satisfy our family's perception of being a genius full of success, then just do your best and you'll get commonly a B.

sections.teaching:
Prof Siu is friendly but it really doesn't mean anything other than getting a good laugh in class. Let me assure you, you will be laughing at a lot of things he said.  Morever, if you like Cantonese accent, he's a good choice (rolls eyes).  He also makes an effort to speak Mandarin to mainland students, which does help boost his popularity as a friendly and/or approachable professor.

Given the grade I give to this part, you see I don't really like it - it's my first course in economics and from there I already wished it was my last.  The worst point is that you would seem to get it, but probably you didn't get it at all... especially when you look at the exam paper and you felt as if you have nowhere to apply the concepts.  I do not think such muddled impressions of the concepts is what good instructors aim to leave in the students' minds.
sections.grading: Let me tell you this - I got at least 2 sd below mean every time and I still got a c+. It's such a miracle.  Your grades would be better if you learnt a bit of microeconomics, have some basic ability to learn new logic and are willing to ask for help when you need it.
sections.workload: You have a midterm and a final exam.  As in other reviews, as long as you submit your homework, whatever you write in there does not matter.  That's true... but if you want a better score, try doing the questions and then ask if you have used the correct approach / gotten the correct answers.
